title: Stakeholders, key influencers and engagement
blurb: Define a stakeholder, find the hidden key influencers, analyse who is impacted and who has influence, and engage them to support change.
question: A project manager's stakeholder list contains only people with project roles. A respected staff representative with no role then turns colleagues against the change. What did PRINCE2 expect the project manager to do?

teach.body: Formally, a stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by the project. In plain English: if they can shape it, feel it, or think they will feel it, they count. Projects must identify stakeholders and key influencers, including key people who are impacted or critical to success but hold no formal role.

The stakeholder analysis, held in the communication management approach, asks who is impacted by the outcome or by the way the project is delivered, and who can influence its success or failure. Interests and attitudes shift as the project moves on, so the analysis is revisited. Pockets of resistance show where communication should be focused: find out why people resist rather than sidelining them.

teach.caption: An illustrative way to sort the analysis, not a PRINCE2 template. The method's point: both impact and influence matter, and a role is not required for either.

teach.body: The way a project is set up should support relationship building across interfaces, for example through regular meetings and working groups that build a shared understanding of different perspectives, the project data and the knowledge stakeholders agree on. From the shared understanding built with key influencers, the project can set ways of working that keep all impacted areas of the organizational ecosystem involved as it progresses.

head: PRINCE2 element
Stakeholder link
teach.caption: Co-creation is collaboration that involves users and key influencers in designing products and ways of working so they are adopted.

teach.body: Kestrel Ridge University is moving its library to 24-hour self-service. Project manager Owen Hughes lists the board, library staff and IT. Then he asks who else could sway success and finds Bev Mallory, the night security supervisor of 20 years, whom staff and students trust. She has no project role, but her doubts about late-night safety are spreading. Owen invites her to a working group on the night-time layout; her ideas are adopted and she becomes an advocate.

teach.text: Stakeholders are not limited to people with project roles, and stakeholder identification is not a one-off at start-up: relationships change over time, and stages often bring new influencers. A pocket of resistance is a signal to investigate and communicate, not a reason to exclude people.

items: Stakeholder: can affect, is affected by, or perceives itself affected by the project (manual 3.2.2).
Identify stakeholders and key influencers, including key people with no formal role.
Stakeholder analysis (communication management approach): who is impacted, who can influence success.
Build relationships across interfaces with regular meetings and working groups that create shared understanding.
Revisit engagement as relationships change; investigate resistance rather than sidelining it.

summary: You can now define a stakeholder, explain why hidden key influencers matter, describe the stakeholder analysis in the communication management approach, and explain how PRINCE2 engages people through shared understanding across interfaces. You can also explain why engagement is revisited as the project moves on.

A.q: Which is the PRINCE2 definition of a stakeholder?
options: Anyone who holds a role within the project management team structure
Anyone who funds the project or will use the products it delivers
Anyone named in the communication schedule for the current stage
Anyone who can affect, be affected by, or perceives they are affected
A.why: A stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by the project (manual 3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Stakeholders include people with no project role, such as affected staff and key influencers.
whyNot.1: Funders and users are stakeholders, but the definition is wider, including anyone affected or perceiving an effect.
whyNot.2: Being in a schedule is a result of analysis, not the definition; people can be stakeholders before they are listed.

A.q: A project manager lists as stakeholders the people with project roles. A respected staff representative with no role later turns colleagues against the change. What should the project manager have done?
options: Identified key people critical to success who hold no formal role
Asked the business layer to give the representative a board seat
Recorded the representative's objection as an off-specification
Raised an exception report when the representative first objected
A.why: PRINCE2 expects the project to identify stakeholders and key influencers, including key people impacted or critical to success who may hold no formal role (manual 3.2.2).

whyNot.1: Engaging an influencer does not mean adding them to the board, which represents business, user and supplier interests.
whyNot.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its specification; an objection is not one.
whyNot.3: Exception reports are for forecast breaches of stage or project tolerance, not stakeholder objections.

A.q: How does PRINCE2 suggest building relationships across interfaces?
options: A launch briefing issued once by the executive to all staff
Regular meetings and working groups that build shared understanding
Escalating each disagreement to the project board for a ruling
Written instructions sent out through approved work packages
A.why: Relationship building across interfaces can be established through regular meetings and working groups that build a shared understanding of perspectives, project data and agreed knowledge (manual 3.2.2).

whyNot.0: A one-off, one-way briefing does not build relationships or shared understanding.
whyNot.2: Escalation is for decisions beyond delegated authority, not a way to build relationships.
whyNot.3: Work packages assign work to teams; they are not a method for building relationships with stakeholders.

B.q:
Which two statements about stakeholder engagement are correct?
1. Stakeholder relationships may change as the project evolves.
2. Stakeholder analysis is completed in starting up and then closed.
3. Key influencers may hold no formal role in the project.
4. Stakeholders who resist should be removed from communications.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Relationships change over time (1), and key influencers can be critical to success without a formal role (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: the analysis is revisited as relationships change, and it sits in the communication management approach agreed in initiation.
whyNot.2: Both are false: analysis is revisited, and resistance should be investigated and communicated with.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: pockets of resistance show where communication should be focused.

B.q: Which management product contains the stakeholder analysis?
options: Change management approach
Sustainability management approach
Communication management approach
Commercial management approach
B.why: The communication management approach includes the stakeholder analysis, alongside the communications schedule and procedures, tools and resources.

whyNot.0: The change management approach describes the states and enabling activities of the transition.
whyNot.1: The sustainability management approach covers the actions, reviews and controls for meeting sustainability targets.
whyNot.3: The commercial management approach covers market engagement, procurement and contract management.

B.q: A group of nurses keeps criticizing a new rota system. Which response best fits PRINCE2's people guidance?
options: Find out why they resist and focus communication there
Exclude them from consultation to protect the timeline
Report the criticism to the board as a tolerance breach
Log the criticism in the issue register as a request for change
B.why: Pockets of resistance show where communication should be focused; the project should investigate the reasons rather than sideline the group.

whyNot.1: Sidelining resistant stakeholders makes adoption less likely; PRINCE2 asks the project to engage them.
whyNot.2: Criticism alone is not a forecast breach of tolerance, so it is not an exception.
whyNot.3: A request for change is a proposal to change a baseline; general criticism is not one.

C.q: Which statement correctly describes the stakeholder analysis in PRINCE2?
options: It lists the risks each stakeholder poses, and it is held in the risk register
It sets each stakeholder's tolerances, and it is held in the project controls
It records who signs off the products, and it is held in the project brief
It finds who is impacted and who can influence success, in the communication approach
C.why: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is impacted by the outcome or delivery process and who can influence success or failure; it is part of the communication management approach.

whyNot.0: The risk register records specific risks; it does not hold the stakeholder analysis.
whyNot.1: Tolerances are set for plans and work packages, not for stakeholders.
whyNot.2: Product sign-off is described in product descriptions and quality responsibilities, not a stakeholder analysis in the brief.

C.q: Why are stage boundaries good points to revisit stakeholder engagement?
options: Stakeholders raise issues at stage boundaries rather than during stages
The stakeholder analysis is first created at the end of each stage
Stages often mark a change in influencers and key relationships
Key influencers join the project board at the start of each stage
C.why: The stages of a project often mark a change in influencers and key relationships, so they are good points to review how people interact (manual 3.5.1).

whyNot.0: Issues can be raised by anyone at any time, not just at stage boundaries.
whyNot.1: The analysis is part of the communication management approach agreed in initiation; it is reviewed, not first created, at stage ends.
whyNot.3: Board membership represents business, user and supplier interests; influencers do not join it at each stage.

C.q: Who does co-creation involve in designing products and agreed ways of working, so that they are adopted?
options: The project board and the business layer
Users and key influencers
Project support and project assurance
Team managers and the change authority
C.why: Co-creation is a specific form of collaboration involving users and key influencers in designing products and agreed ways of working so they are adopted (manual 3.3).

whyNot.0: The board directs and the business layer commissions; co-creation is defined around users and key influencers.
whyNot.2: Support and assurance roles help run and check the project; they are not the focus of co-creation.
whyNot.3: Team managers deliver products and a change authority approves changes; co-creation centres on users and key influencers.

reteach.title: Planning a village fete
reteach.question: Organizing a village fete, would you talk only to the committee, or also to the people whose say-so really moves the village?

blocks.body: The fete committee holds the formal roles. But the publican, the head teacher and the neighbour who runs the village social media page can make or break it, with no committee role at all. The organizer who meets them early, listens to their worries and plans together gets their support. Leave them out and resistance spreads. That is stakeholder engagement with key influencers.

blocks.text: Holding a role is not the test for being a stakeholder or a key influencer. Effect, perceived effect and influence are.

explain.body: Projects must involve those with formal roles and key people who are impacted by the project or critical to its success, even though they may hold no formal role. Those are often the key influencers.

test.q: Which statement about key influencers is correct?
options: They may be critical to success without a formal role
They are the members of the project board
They are appointed to the project by the business layer
They are listed in the project management team structure
test.why: Key influencers can be critical to the success of the project without holding any formal role, so they must be identified deliberately.

whyNot.1: Board members are role holders; key influencers are often outside any formal role.
whyNot.2: The business layer appoints the executive; key influencers are not appointed.
whyNot.3: The PMT structure shows project roles, which many key influencers do not hold.

explain.body: The stakeholder analysis asks who is impacted by the outcome or by the delivery process, and who can influence the project's success or failure. It is part of the communication management approach.

test.q: Which question does a PRINCE2 stakeholder analysis answer?
options: Which products need a quality review before approval?
How large should the change budget be for this stage?
Which risks are forecast to exceed the risk tolerance?
Who can influence the project's success or failure?
test.why: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is impacted and who can influence success or failure.

whyNot.0: Quality review planning belongs to the quality practice.
whyNot.1: The change budget is set by the board under the issues practice.
whyNot.2: Risk tolerance is part of the risk practice.

explain.body: Build relationships across interfaces through regular meetings and working groups that create shared understanding of perspectives, project data and agreed knowledge. From that shared understanding with key influencers, set ways of working that keep impacted areas involved.

test.q: What should engagement across interfaces build, according to PRINCE2?
options: A single approved view set by the executive
A record of the tolerances agreed with each stakeholder group
A shared understanding of perspectives and project data
A list of who to escalate each disagreement to
test.why: Meetings and working groups should build a shared understanding of different perspectives, the project data and the knowledge stakeholders agree on.

whyNot.0: Engagement aims at shared understanding, not a view imposed by one person.
whyNot.1: Tolerances are set for plans and work packages, not agreed with stakeholder groups.
whyNot.3: Escalation routes are part of governance; engagement is about shared understanding.

explain.body: Relationships change over time and stages often bring new influencers. Revisit who matters and how they are engaged, especially at stage boundaries.

test.q: A project moves from design into roll-out, and regional managers suddenly become influential. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the original analysis, since it was baselined in the PID
Revisit stakeholder identification and key relationships
Raise an exception report to the project board
Ask the regional managers to act as the change authority
test.why: Relationships and influencers change over the project, so identification and engagement should be revisited.

whyNot.0: Baselined approaches are reviewed and updated, for example at stage boundaries; they are not frozen.
whyNot.2: New influencers are not a forecast breach of tolerance.
whyNot.3: A change authority approves requests for change; it is not a way to engage influencers.
